question: A chest X-ray in a 55-year-old immunocompetent patient with CAP shows a right upper-lobe opacity with air-bronchogram and mild volume loss. Which pattern and pathogen association is most consistent with this finding?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Classic lobar consolidation from S. pneumoniae typically does not cause volume loss; upper-lobe involvement with cavity or volume loss in an immunocompetent host suggests a different pathogen.

answers.text: Upper-lobe opacity with volume loss — Mycobacterium tuberculosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Upper-lobe infiltrates with volume loss (and potential cavitation) in an immunocompetent adult in India must first raise the suspicion of pulmonary TB. ATT cover rather than standard pneumonia antibiotics is considered once TB is excluded.
Mycoplasma typically produces a bilateral interstitial or patchy bronchopneumonia pattern, not a unilateral upper-lobe opacity with volume loss.
PCP causes bilateral perihilar ground-glass infiltrates and is almost exclusively seen in immunocompromised patients (HIV with CD4 <200); this patient is immunocompetent.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the Indian caveat: any upper-lobe opacity with volume loss or cavitation in an immunocompetent host is TB until proved otherwise. The CXR pattern + clinical context (upper lobe, volume loss, Indian setting) should trigger a TB workup before or alongside standard CAP treatment.

Well done. In the Indian context, upper-lobe opacity with volume loss or cavitation must be presumed TB until proved otherwise; empirical anti-pneumococcal therapy alone is inadequate — send sputum AFB/GeneXpert and consider TB overlap before initiating treatment.
